statement: A CDN transparently sits between your user and your origin.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So the way CDN works is that it transparently sits between your user and your origin.

statement: A CDN is not something you push things to, and it is not merely 'there to cache things': although CDNs now offer APIs, pushing content is not their main motive - the CDN sits transparently in front of the origin.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: No, I'll push things to CDN. CDN is not something where you push things. Although now they offer APIs, but that's not their main motive.

statement: Origin is a generic term for where the content lives - an S3 bucket, a backend server, literally anything you want served via your CDN.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Origin is where your origin is, which means where either your S3 bucket, either your backend server, anything, literally anything that you want to...

statement: The origin needs to be publicly accessible; some security policies can be applied, depending on the CDN you use.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now, origin needs to be publicly accessible. You can apply some security policies there.

statement: Example: the origin is the teacher's website arpitbhayani.me and some part of it, e.g. the image at arpitbhayani.me/systemdesign/logo.png, should be served via CDN; the content could be JSON, bytes, an image, HTML or video.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Let's say that image's path is arpitbhayani.me slash systemdesign slash logo.png. So this is that image path.

statement: Without a CDN, hitting the image URL resolves the domain to the origin's IP (a load balancer), which forwards the request to a backend server that reads the image and sends it back to the user.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: arpitbhayani.me's domain name will be resolved to an IP address, resolution would happen. Which IP address would it resolve to? It would resolve to...

statement: Images are almost static data: they rarely change once they are there, so spending backend server bandwidth on them is wasteful.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So the bandwidth of my backend server is getting consumed for something which is almost static images. How frequently would they change? Not really.

statement: Images are huge (1, 2, 3, 5, 10 MB); consuming 10 MB of API-server bandwidth to serve one is 'a crime' - you want your API servers to be lean and fast.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now imagine transferring, consuming 10MB worth of bandwidth of your API servers. That's a crime. You want your API servers to be lean and fast.

statement: Instead of the backend transferring the data, another component can take care of it and distribute it geographically, caching the content near the user - that is exactly what a CDN is.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: What if that other thing distributes it geographically? Now that is an advantage.

statement: If the server sits in Singapore and a user in the US accesses it, transferring a 10 MB image to the US slows things down; caching the image near the user fixes that.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Transferring 10 MB of image to US will slow things down. What if the 10 MB image is cached near to that user?

statement: On a CDN provider you configure a mapping called a CDN property: your subdomain on the provider (e.g. a.mycdn.net) mapped to an origin (e.g. arpitbhayani.me), meaning any request to a.mycdn.net is forwarded to arpitbhayani.me.
detail: The content chosen for the CDN is the near-static, huge part (images).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is the mapping that you configure on CDN that, hey, this is my CDN property. a.mycdn.net mapped with arpitbhayani.me.

statement: The part of a website to serve via CDN is the part that is near static and huge in size, such as images.

statement: The browser does not know whether a host is a CDN: it does DNS resolution of whatever hostname is in the URL and forwards the request to that IP address.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Doesn't know it's a CDN or browser, it's simple, whatever the host name is, I'll do the DNS resolution, I'll forward the request to...

statement: DNS resolution of the CDN hostname (a.mycdn.net) returns the CDN provider's IP address; this is classic DNS configuration done on Route 53 or a domain provider such as GoDaddy or Namecheap.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The domain name resolution will spit out the IP address of the CDN provider

statement: When the CDN receives a request for a.mycdn.net/<path>, it looks up the origin configured for that property, replaces the CDN host with the origin (arpitbhayani.me) and requests the same path from the origin.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It will check in the mapping. What is a.mycdn.net configured to as an origin?

statement: You do not have to configure every URL on the CDN: literally any path under the CDN property works, because the CDN carries the path over to the origin.

statement: On the first request for a path, the CDN has nothing cached, so the CDN itself makes the request to the origin (arpitbhayani.me/systemdesign/logo.png); the origin generates the response as it always does, and the CDN caches it and sends it to the user.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: CDN first check, hey, do I have anything cache for this path? No, because it's a first request.

statement: On the next request for the same path the CDN already has the image cached and serves it directly; if it did not, it would go to the origin, grab it and serve it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It has this image cache that we directly serve it over here.

statement: That is all a CDN does: you configure a CDN property and an origin; for any path it serves cached data if it has it, otherwise fetches the same path from the origin and serves it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If it does not, it goes to the origin for the same path, gets a response and serves it. That's it. That's all CDN does.

statement: Geographical distribution and similar features are advanced configuration; the bare minimum a normal engineer building a system needs is the CDN sitting transparently in between.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Geographical distribution and all those are advanced configuration, but this is the bare minimum where your CDN sits transparently in between.

statement: A CDN does not care whether the response is an image or a video: whatever it gets in the response it caches as a set of bytes, so you can cache API responses, JSON responses, text files, images, videos and fragments on a CDN.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: For CDN, it is just set of bytes, which is the beauty of it.

statement: A common belief is that only images can be cached on a CDN; in fact for a CDN it is literally just a set of bytes.

verbatim: I can only cache images on CDN. No. For CDN, it's literally just a set of bytes.

statement: Giphy leverages CDN beautifully and caches a lot of stuff on it; the teacher has a YouTube video on how Giphy uses CDN.

statement: A CDN does not even let the request come into the backend infrastructure when it has the content, saving backend bandwidth and reducing infrastructure cost: you need only a couple of servers instead of hundreds, with only a few requests reaching the backend each time the cache invalidates.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: what CDN helps us achieve is that it does not even let the request come within the backend infra.

statement: You pay the CDN money because it gives efficiency and reduces backend load: you keep infrastructure cost down while paying almost an equivalent amount to the CDN, and get extra performance.

verbatim: You keep your infrastructure cost down while paying almost equivalent amount of money to CDN and to get extra performance.

statement: System design is all about building blocks: once you know how a solution works you can Ctrl-C, Ctrl-V it anywhere - GitHub's attachment upload and Instagram's image upload are one and the same.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: That's why I say system design is all about building blocks.

statement: GitHub demo: attaching an image (179 KB PNG) to an issue comment triggers four network calls; the first goes to github.com/upload/policies/assets, registering the intent to upload with the image upload service.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it made the request to github.com slash upload slash policy slash assets. It means that it is creating, it is registering

statement: The first request sends only metadata - image name, size (183938 bytes = 179 KB), content type image/png and an authentication token; the image itself is not yet sent.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The first request is now sent from user, your front end, to github.com's backend, and here image is not yet sent.
flags: check: file name as read from screen

statement: The response contains a signed upload URL which is not a GitHub URL but S3's URL, generated via S3, with all the information the frontend needs to upload the image directly to S3.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's not GitHub URL. It is S3's URL.

statement: The response's asset href - the future image URL - is a CDN URL on user-images.githubusercontent.com (GitHub's CDN alias, like edge.arpitbhayani.me), whose path contains the image ID (221335625).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This HREF is what your image URL is going to be. If you look carefully, this is the CDN URL.

statement: On upload intent the backend optionally makes a database entry, gets a random image ID, builds the S3 path (folder/ID.png), creates a pre-signed URL for it, and exposes the CDN URL rather than the actual S3 path; that CDN URL is used to render the image.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So it did not expose the actual S3 path. It exposed the CDN URL

statement: GitHub inserts the image as standard markdown with an exclamation mark at the beginning, which means render it as an image.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this is how it would render put by an exclamation mark at the beginning which means render it as an image. Standard markdown format.

statement: The response's form object contains what S3 needs; when uploading directly to S3 you pass these fields in the body of the HTTP POST so S3 knows it is a pre-signed upload. This is specific to S3, but GCP and Azure blob storage have equivalent patterns; the concept is the same.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But the idea, the concept, the logic remains the same.

statement: The upload URL itself is just the normal S3 bucket endpoint; what makes the upload pre-signed is the set of fields passed in the body of the POST request.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But this is normal S3's endpoint. This is my S3 bucket path like bucket endpoint. Like is where is pre-signed URL?

statement: The 'key' field is the path in the S3 bucket at which the pre-signed URL was generated and where the image is uploaded - the same path as in the CDN URL.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The key. This is the path in S3 from the bucket.

statement: The ACL field 'public-read' makes the created object readable by everyone without authentication or special certificates; ACLs can be changed.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Then this is ACL public read, that this image, this part that I'm creating is readable by everyone.

statement: The 'policy' field is the signed certificate, signed with the S3 key held on the API server; it embeds the expiration, so S3 needs no database or timer to decide validity - once the time has passed, the upload is not allowed. JWTs work in a similar way.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It does not maintain a database to store the time and all. It does it with expiration embedded in this thing.

statement: The remaining fields - Amazon algorithm, credential, date, signature - are parameters AWS wants in the request.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Amazon algorithm, credential, date, signature. These are all AWS. These are parameters that AWS wants in the request that you make it.

statement: The second step: the frontend makes a POST to github-production-user-asset...s3.amazonaws.com (S3's URL) with form data - key, ACL, policy, algorithm, content type - taken from the first response, plus the file with the actual image bytes (about 173 KB of PNG); the image goes directly to S3.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Post request goes to what? github hyphen production hyphen user hyphen asset dot
flags: asr: [?s3.amazonaws.com | asr: "s dot a amazon aws.com"]

statement: What happens after the upload (rendering the image) is GitHub's own logic; what makes this flow special is how it saved bandwidth.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: What makes this thing special is how we saved bandwidth.

statement: Opening the image URL goes to the CDN (user-images.githubusercontent.com); the first time the CDN lacks the path, so it goes to the origin GitHub configured - the S3 bucket - reads the key, caches it and forwards it to the user; the next load comes from the CDN and is faster.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: CDN will go to S3. Why? Because GitHub folks configured on their CDN that, hey, this is the origin for this.

statement: Image upload practically everywhere (Instagram, GitHub attachments) always uses pre-signed URLs, because it saves a ton of bandwidth.
case_study: Instagram image upload is the running case study.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Everywhere, it is always pre-signed URL because it saves a ton of bandwidth for us. And that's why everyone prefers it.

statement: Submitting the GitHub issue is like publishing an Instagram post: the image is first uploaded to S3, ready to be published, then a separate post call publishes it - the same flow as Instagram.
case_study: Instagram image upload is the running case study.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: First your image is there, uploaded on S3, ready to be published. Then when you post, this is what happens behind the scenes.

statement: Q: How is content moderation done in this flow? A: It is a different system, done with asynchronous processing; if moderation must happen in the request context before publishing, you cannot upload directly to S3 - which is why most moderation happens after the image is published or almost on the fly.
case_study: Instagram image upload is the running case study.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If you're doing content moderation before you are allowed to publish, then you cannot do it before.

statement: Q: Where does the CDN URL in the upload response come from? A: The backend image upload service generates it: the path stays the same and you prefix it with your CDN endpoint, i.e. replace the S3 bucket name with the CDN host - plain string concatenation.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You just replace your S3 path, that S3 bucket name, with your CDN thing and then that's your CDN path.

statement: Q: Why does the response include the CDN URL and not only the pre-signed S3 URL? A: So that the frontend knows what URL to render; S3 is not public - you cannot just call the S3 URL to get the data; it is only allowed for the CDN.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Because S3 is not public. S3 URL is not public. You cannot just make call to S3 URL and get the data.

statement: Q: Why is a CDN faster than S3 - e.g. CDN in Mumbai vs S3 in Bangalore? A: That is a very specific example; if Akamai has an edge server in Bangalore, the CDN. The key reason is geography, though there may be other optimizations - do a benchmark to find out.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Key reason is geography, but there might be other things. Do a benchmark and find it out

detail: The teacher hedges on CDN internals ('I don't know where they are storing', 'CDN might have a bunch of SSDs. We don't know') but also says 'CDN uses SSD'.

statement: S3 and CDNs give different guarantees: S3 gives something like a nine-nines guarantee (durability), whereas a CDN gives better response time.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: S3 gives you nine nines guarantee, something like that. Right. CDN gives you different guarantees. They give you better response time.

statement: If you want to squeeze out performance, benchmark and see what works best for you; if the CDN does not work best that is okay, but then you pay S3's egress cost and should be okay with that.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If CDN does not work best for you, that's okay. Right. But then you will have to pay for S3's egress cost.

statement: Q: Does the CDN need a signed URL to fetch from S3? A: Only for private images; otherwise it can access directly. For a private S3 bucket, the CDN's AWS integration lets you upload an AWS access key and secret key to the CDN so it can read the private images.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: No, if it's a private image, then you need a signed URL to do that. Otherwise you can directly access.

statement: A student assumed the CDN fetching a private image from S3 goes through the same flow, generating a signed URL.
detail: Correction: it does not - the CDN holds AWS access and secret keys and does a normal S3 read with the AWS SDK, not via a URL.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: No, it does not. It has AWS access keys and secret keys. It can directly make an S3 call to read it.

statement: Keys on the CDN are one way but maybe not the only one: because almost everyone uses a CDN in front of S3, CDNs have native S3 integrations and S3 supports seamless CDN integration, without per-request authentication.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: CDN has native integrations on S3 and S3 also by default supports seamless integration with CDN
